McDonalds' Menu Analysis¶

Image source ("McDs.png")

This project was completed in September, 2025.¶

📖 Background¶

McDonalds is an American-based, international fast-food chain that has served meals & snacks to customers since the 1940's. Over time, their menu has grown to include a large variety of foods including burgers, beverages, breakfast foods, chicken, fish, coffee, salads, desserts, & more. They are one of the most well-known food chains in the world.

In the mid-1990's, the United States Food & Drug Administration (FDA) passed into the law the requirement for food packages to contain detailed information about a food item's nutrients, serving size, calories, & such. Consequentially, McDonalds has provided various nutritional facts on their menus for each of their food items that they offer such as calories, carbohydrates, sodium, fat, etc. Such information can be explored to understand what McDonalds items are made of, how effectively they can contribute to a typicaly, daily diet, & how healthy they might be.

The dataset was obtained from Kaggle (unfortunately, this link doesn't exist anymore). While it may not reflect current food items on the McDonalds menu, it still contains an extensive variety of foods.

💾 The Data¶

The dataset contains nutritional information & other details of items across the McDonalds menu as seen below. At the time in which the data was obtained, it contained 260 unique menu items. Nutritional notes & recommendations from the US FDA were also incorporated.
Note that the variables that quantify percentages of daily values of nutrients that menu items account for are based on a 2,000-calorie daily diet.

Variable Description
Category The category of the food item. They include Breakfast, Beef & Pork, Chicken & Fish, Salads, Snacks & Sides, Desserts, Beverages, Coffee & Tea, Smoothies & Shakes.
Item The name of the food item as listed on the McDonalds' menu.
Serving Size The recommended serving size of each food item. Most items contain multiple measurements with different units that consist of ounces, grams, fluid ounces, milliliters, or others. These values depend on the item type.
Calories The estimated number of calories the food item has in a single serving.
Calories from Fat The estimated number of calories from fat the food item has in a single serving.
Total Fat The estimated amount of fat (in grams) the food item has in a single serving.
Total Fat (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of total fat that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.
Saturated Fat The estimated amount of saturated fat (in grams) the food item has in a single serving.
Saturated Fat (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of saturated fat that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.
Trans Fat The estimated amount of trans fat (in grams) the food item has in a single serving.
Cholesterol The estimated cholesterol (in milligrams) the food item has in a single serving.
Cholesterol (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of cholesterol that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.
Sodium The estimated amount of sodium (in milligrams) the food item has in a single serving.
Sodium (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of sodium that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.
Carbohydrates The estimated amount of carbohydrates (in grams) the food item has in a single serving.
Carbohydrates (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of carbohydrates that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.
Dietary Fiber The estimated amount of dietary fiber (in grams) the food item has in a single serving.
Dietary Fiber (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of dietary fiber that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.
Sugars The estimated amount of sugars (in grams) the food item has in a single serving.
Protein The estimated amount of protein (in grams) the food item has in a single serving.
Vitamin A (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of vitamin A that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.
Vitamin C (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of vitamin C that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.
Calcium (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of calcium that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.
Iron (% Daily Value) The estimated percentage of iron that the food item accounts for in a typical person's daily diet.

Objectives¶

With this data, various contents & details of different food items on the McDonalds menu can be analyzed. Create a report that investigates the following objectives. 1) Find foods that exceed any recommended nutritional daily value. 2) Find the five food items with the most nutritional value across each nutritional element. 3) Inspect the typical amount of each nutrient per category in the McDonalds menu. 4) Construct a daily meal plan that doesn't exceed the recommended daily nutritional values; i.e. breakfast, lunch, & dinner. Include at least eight unique food items. Assume that the daily nutritional values are for a 2,000 calorie (daily) diet.

Summary of Findings¶

This project analyzed various details & nutritional information of items across the vast McDonalds menu. Food items were assessed individually & across categories to determine how they contribute to a typical daily diet across various nutritional elements. Through these analyses, items that exceed daily recommendations in terms of nutrients were identified. As an exercise, daily meal plans were built from the McDonalds menu to try & satisfy a healthy distribution of daily nutrients.

Many fast-food chains are known for the richness & abundance in their foods. While they excel at quickly producing & providing such foods, they are not typically known for being healthy in terms of thir food. Prior to such analyses, recommended quantities of daily nutrients, according to the McDonalds menu items, were compared to those of the US Food & Drug Administration, a source that is likely to be more focused on providing safe, credible, healthy information. This was done to determine if McDonalds' daily recommendations & calculations were appropriate & how healthy they might be.
Of the nutritional elements that are in common across these two sources, some had very similar recommendations whereas others did not. More specifically, recommended daily amounts of saturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, & dietary fiber across these two sources were within no more than three grams of each other. Conversely, there was a 13-gram difference & a 25-gram difference in the recommended daily amounts of total fat & carbohydrates respectively (McDonalds recommended less total fat but more carbohydrates).
Ultimately, given the level of similarity between these nutrients & their recommendations, it was determined that the daily recommendations from McDonalds' menu items were adequate in terms of accuracy & how they quantify a typical daily, healthy diet.

Analysis I - Rich Foods¶

Find foods that exceed any recommended nutritional daily value.

Various individuals have different needs & desires in terms of how they want to consume food & nutrients; however, there are definitely levels of healthy & unhealthy. For example, if a single food item from McDonalds accounts for 95 percent of a typical diet's recommended daily total fat, it would be considered to be unhealthy because of how disproportionate it is in contributing to the consumer's total fat for a day. By identifying such foods that are exceptionally or excessively rich in nutrition, it can indicate whether such foods, in isolation, are generally unhealthy in some way.

  • In particular, the US FDA advises to consume foods that are higher in dietary fiber & lower in saturated fat, sodium, & added sugars.

This section assesses these points by utilizing the variables that describe nutritional values relative to a recommended daily value such as such as the 'Total Fat (% Daily Value)' variable. Since these daily-value estimates are based off of a daily diet that consumes 2,000 calories, such a diet was considered to be generally "healthy" for the purposes of this analysis; however, that is not to say that all other diets are unequivocally unhealthy.

Of the 260 food items in the menu, 21 of them exceed one or more nutrients in terms of how much they account for in a single serving. In this selection of items, the nutrients which saw excessive amounts in a single serving include total fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, vitamin A, & vitamin C. Of these items, seven are breakfast foods, six are salads, & four are beverages. There were two items that include an overabundance in terms of the daily recommended amounts of multiple nutrients.

  • One serving of "Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Large Biscuit)" accounts for about 100 percent of a typical daily diet's recommended saturated fat level & about 192 percent of the recommended daily amount of cholesterol.
  • One serving of the "40-piece Chicken McNuggets" accounts for about 182 percent of a typical daily diet's recommended total fat level, about 101 percent of the recommended daily amount of saturated fat, & about 150 percent of the recommended daily amount of sodium.

Many of these 21 items contain very unbalanced amounts of nutrients. In consuming such items, not only can it put the consumer "over their daily limit" when it comes to certain nutrients, but it also compromises what other foods they might eat over the rest of the day if they are trying to follow a balanced diet. While there are certainly foods that can help balance out these richer items in terms of nutrients, consuming them will make it more challenging for a consumer to properly balance their diet due to how disproportionate they are in their nutritional balance.

With this in mind, if people are looking to avoid consuming excessive amounts of certain nutrients, they would be advised to avoid these foods or get them in smaller quantities, particularly those high in saturated fat, sodium, & added sugars. Conversely, for those with a desire to consume greater amounts of certain nutrients, particularly total fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, vitamin A, & vitamin C, these items might be viable options.

Analysis II - Rich Foods by Nutrient¶

Find the five food items with the most nutritional value across each nutrient.

In an extension of Analysis I, the five most abundant foods across each nutrient were obtained & analyzed to assess how McDonalds foods generally contribute to nutritional balance. Daily recommendations from the US FDA were used to assess how extreme items were in their nutritional abundances.

Overall, the 40-piece Chicken McNuggets has the most nutritional value for four different nutrients (calories, total fat, sodium, protein) which is more than any other food item on the McDonalds menu. Other items with significantly large values across multiple nutrients include: Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Large & Regular Biscuits), Medium McFlurry w/M&M's Candies, Premium Southwest Salad with Crispy Chicken, Premium Southwest Salad with Gilled Chicken, Large Strawberry Shake, Large Chocolate Shake, & other Big Breakfast food items.

In short, McDonalds seems to offer several items that are generally either very rich, moderately heavy, or underwhelming in terms of their nutritional abundances across the nutrients analyzed.

  • Nutrients in which several McDonalds items are generally very rich in include: Saturated Fat, Cholesterol, Sodium, Sugars, Vitamin A, & Vitamin C.
  • Nutrients in which several McDonalds items are generally moderately heavy in include: Calories, Total Fat, Trans Fat, Carbohydrates, Protein, & Calcium.
  • Nutrients in which several McDonalds items are generally underwhelming include: Dietary Fiber & Iron.

With this in mind, people who are desiring to follow a balanced diet would be advised that they may need to be more strict in what they consume from McDonalds when it comes to saturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, sugars, vitamin A, & vitamin C. They would also be advised that there are several items that are moderately heavy in calories, total fat, trans fat, carbohydrates, protein, & calcium. On the other hand, such customers don't necessarily have to be concerned about consuming excessive levels of dietary fiber & iron when eating from McDonalds; however, customers who want to consume more fiber &/or iron than a typical diet may recommend may find McDonalds' selection of items insufficient.
When evaluated against particular recommendations from the US FDA, these analyses seem to indicate that McDonalds foods generally provide unhealthy amounts of saturated fat, sodium, & sugars & insufficient amounts of dietary fiber & iron. Across these six particular nutrients, McDonalds foods only seem satisfactory when it comes to calcium levels.

Analysis III - Nutrients by Food Category¶

Inspect the typical amount of each nutrient per category in the McDonalds menu.

Breaking down nutritional abundances by category in the McDonalds menu can help reveal typical nutritional compositions of such items. These distributions can potentially be helpful in informing customers & how they can consume a more balanced collection of foods when eating at McDonalds. For example, if a customer consumes an item high in cholesterol, having an understanding of nutrients in other items can help assist them in assessing what other foods they could eat that aren't as high in cholesterol. Such information could also be useful for people who are following more particular diets such as high-protein or low-fat diets.

In the dataset, there are nine unique categories each of which accounts for between six & 95 food items on the menu. When assessing measures of centrality, the median was used given that it is less sensitive to outliers.

Of the 14 nutrients that were examined, some categories consistently have some of the largest nutritional abundances.

  • McDonalds Smoothies & Shakes & Beef & Pork items each have the highest typical quantities across four of the 14 nutrients. Smoothies & Shakes are typically the most abundant in calories, carbs, sugars, & calcium, whereas Beef & Pork food items are typically the most abundant in fat, trans fat, cholesterol, & iron. Moreover, Chicken & Fish as well as Breakfast items are also fairly rich in terms of nutritional abundance.
  • Conversely, McDonalds Beverages are usually among the least fulfilling of the nine categories across most of these nutrients (11 of 14). Snacks & Sides & Desserts items are also typically less sufficient in supplying adequate amounts of nutrients.

When assessing how extreme food categories from McDonalds typically were across these nutrients, there were two instances in which a category exceeded the daily recommendation of a nutrient. More specifically, Salads typically exceeded the recommended amount of vitamin A (165%) that should be consumed in a day, & Smoothies & Shakes (75 g) typically exceeded the recommended amount of sugars (50 g). Moreover, multiple categories also typically contained fairly heavy abundances of various nutrients particularly saturated fat, sodium, & protein. On the other hand, there were a few nutrients in which many food categories typically fail to provide adequate amounts specifically dietary fiber, vitamin A, vitamin C, & iron.

In regard to the nutrients most emphasized by the US FDA:

  • Breakfast, Beef & Pork, & Smoothies & Shakes items from McDonalds are particularly rich in saturated fat. Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with less saturated fat, such items would generally be considered unhealthy.
  • Breakfast, Chicken & Fish, & Beef & Pork items from McDonalds are fairly rich in sodium. Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with less sodium, such items would generally be considered unhealthy.
  • Smoothies & Shakes & Coffee & Tea items from McDonalds are fairly rich in sugars. Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with less added sugars, such items would generally be considered unhealthy.
  • The greatest abundance in dietary fiber of the nine McDonalds food categories is about 4.5 grams (Salads). Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with more dietary fiber (the daily recommendation is about 28 grams), McDonalds foods generally seem to lack adequate amounts of dietary fiber.
  • Three McDonalds food categories typically contain between 20 to 40 percent of the daily recommended value of calcium (Smoothies & Shakes, Coffee & Tea, & Beef & Pork). While these categories are somewhat sufficient in providing customers with adequate amounts of calcium--a nutrient in which the FDA encourages people to consume more of--the other six categories, most of which are non-drink categories, are not.
  • The greatest abundance in iron of the nine McDonalds food categories is about 20% of the daily recommended value (Beef & Pork & Chicken & Fish). Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with more iron, McDonalds foods generally seem to lack adequate amounts of iron.

Analysis IV - Assessing Nutrition of Daily Meals¶

Construct a daily meal plan that doesn't exceed the recommended daily nutritional values; i.e. breakfast, lunch, & dinner. Include at least eight unique food items. Assume that the daily nutritional values are for a 2,000 calorie diet.

By constructing daily meal plans using various McDonalds foods, it can give an idea as to how healthy McDonalds foods generally are. Moreover, it can indicate whether McDonalds foods are generally more biased towards certain nutrients or not & whether they are generally capable of providing customers with well-balanced meals.

Two approaches were used in this section as listed below. The daily nutritional recommendations & limits used to guide these analyses were based off of those outlined by the US FDA & some defined based on McDonalds' daily value percentages. 1) Random daily meals were assembled to evaluate how & if a day's worth of McDonalds food satisfies daily nutritional recommendations. 2) The food items were explored to manually construct a day's worth of McDonalds food such that none of the daily nutritional recommendations were excessively exceeded.

Analysis IV A - Random Daily Meal Plans¶

The first approach randomly assembled daily meal plans by sampling items from the various McDonalds food categories based on what items people typically eat throughout a day. For example, a random breakfast & coffee item could be chosen for a typical breakfast meal, whereas a random salad & beverage item could be sampled for a typical lunch meal. By assembling multiple meal plans, it could help assess how daily meal plans from McDonalds typically contribute towards a consumer's daily nutrition & whether they are generally balanced or not.

Ten random daily meal plans were assembled each of which consisted of eight items from the McDonalds menu. Of the ten daily meal plans, at least three of them exceeded the daily recommended quantity for at least 13 of the 15 nutrients analyzed. Furthermore, at least eight meal plans exceeded the daily recommendations for nine of the nutrients. The two nutrients whose daily values were never exceeded in any daily meal plan were dietary fiber & iron. Moreover, daily recommendations of trans fat & vitamin C were only exceeded in four of the ten daily meal plans. Given this information, some conclusions can be made regarding a typical day's worth of McDonalds food items.

  • McDonalds meals usually fail to provide enough dietary fiber & iron for a balanced daily diet.
  • McDonalds meals often provide excessive amounts of calcium, calories, calories from fat, carbohydrates, protein, saturated fat, sodium, sugars, & total fat.
  • McDonalds meals sometimes provide too much cholesterol, trans fat, vitamin A, & vitamin C than a balanced daily diet typically requires.

Of the six nutrients specifically pointed out by the US FDA (dietary fiber, calcium, iron, saturated fat, sodium, & sugars), the analyses indicate that typical McDonalds meals are only sufficient in regard to one of them. More specifically, McDonalds meals typically provide ample amounts of calcium which is more desirable than the opposite according to the FDA; however, McDonalds meals typically provide insufficient amounts of dietary fiber & iron & excessive amounts of saturated fat, sodium, & sugars.
As such, it can be said that McDonalds meals typically fail to provide appropriate amounts of nutrients for balanced, healthy diets.

Analysis IV B - Manually Constructed Meal Plan¶

Next, an eleventh daily meal plan was built, this time by hand, such that the recommended daily nutritional quantities were not grossly excessive or insufficient. This process was tinkered with until the entire collection of food items did not exceed any recommended daily nutritional values. Once more, a day's worth of meals consisted of eight items (listed below) from the McDonalds items spread across three unique meals for breakfast, lunch, & dinner.
Through this, it can be determined as to how difficult assembling a balanced daily meal plan of McDonalds foods generally is & what nutrients consumers may need to look elsewhere for otherwise.

  • This daily meal plan included: Hotcakes, an Iced Coffee with Sugar Free French Vanilla Syrup (Medium), a Diet Dr Pepper (Large), a Filet-O-Fish, Small French Fries, a Hamburger, a Dasani Water Bottle, & a Chocolate Chip Cookie.

In the meal plan that was assembled, it was determined that while the items provide adequate amounts of several nutrients, they underwhelmed for some others particularly those emphasized by the US FDA. In a daily meal plan that contains about 1,490 calories (about three-quarters of a typical daily diet), the foods provide fairly adequate amounts of calories from fat, protein, saturated fat, sodium, sugars, total fat, & trans fat. Conversely, they underwhelm appreciably when it comes to calcium, cholesterol, dietary fiber, iron, vitamin A, & vitamin C.

Regarding the six nutrients particularly emphasized by the US FDA (dietary fiber, iron, calcium, saturated fat, sodium, & sugars), these meals are fairly rich in saturated fat, sodium, & sugars. Given that these items account for at least 84% of the daily recommended quantities but only about 75% in terms of calories, they provide somewhat excessive amounts of saturated fat, sodium, & sugars which might be indicative of unhealthy food options given that such levels of these nutrients are particularly discouraged by the FDA.
Moreover, these meals are quite insufficient in dietary fiber, iron, & calcium--nutrients in which the FDA encourages people to consume more of.

As such, given the uneven proportions in nutrients, particularly of those emphasized by the US FDA, this daily meal plan leans more towards being unhealthy & unbalanced based on a typical diet; however, there is still enough room, in terms of calories, such that these imbalances can be righted, but consumers may need to go beyond McDonalds to find suitable food items. Moreover, for those trying to follow a healthier, more balanced diet, eating these eight items will likely make it more challenging for them to find healthier foods that can supplement these items without exceeding certain nutrients that these foods are relatively rich in.

In relation to Analysis IV A, in which ten random daily meal plans were assembled, this eleventh meal plan seems to be a slight outlier in some aspects given that it did not exceed any daily nutritional recommendations, whereas all but two nutrients & their recommendations were exceeded across many of the former ten meal plans. This might be indicative as to how challenging it generally is to assemble a day's worth of meals from McDonalds that can generate a balanced diet in terms of nutrients.

In the original dataset, there are 260 rows & 24 columns. Each row corresponds to a unique McDonalds food item that was previously or is currently present on their menu. There are no missing values in the dataset.

Many of the nutritional columns do not display any corresponding units. It would be helpful to have these available, especially when presenting analyses to unfamiliar audiences. To determine these units, these products & their corresponding nutritional values could be searched for online. One source could be the McDonalds' website. The relevant nutrients have the following units:

  • Grams (g): fat, carbohydrates, dietary fiber, added sugars, protein
  • Milligrams (mg): cholesterol, sodium

Daily Nutrition¶

There are several columns in the dataset that describe the quantity of some nutritional value in regards to a daily value, such as the 'Total Fat (% Daily Value)' column. It would be valuable to know McDonalds' assessment of these daily values to understand what kind of diet they might be basing their nutrition facts off of & if such a diet is healthy. As a start, McDonalds' current website states that the percentages of daily values (DV) are based on a 2,000 calorie diet; however, such a diet could vary in a plethora ways across other nutritional quantities (e.g. carbohydrates, protein, sodium, etc.).

For consistency purposes, it would be useful to get a detailed breakdown of a typical 2,000 calorie diet & what the recommended values are for the various different nutritional quantities. With such values, they could be valuable for analyses that may use this data to understand how different food items might make up a typical daily diet. For example, if someone had a typical meal at McDonalds, how much of their daily nutrition might be satisfied by such a meal?

To achieve this, the nutritional variables with associated daily percentage values could be used to calculate McDonalds' understanding of the recommended daily values for such quantities. Additionally, a second source, such as the US Food & Drug Administration (FDA), could help in crosschecking these values to gain a better understanding of McDonalds' typical daily nutritional recommendations & how appropriate they may be.

  • This information can be referenced in the FDA_daily_nuts.csv file.

In the dataset, there are six nutrients that have variables pertaining to both an absolute quantity & a daily-value quantity including 'Total Fat,' 'Saturated Fat,' 'Cholesterol,' 'Sodium,' 'Carbohydrates,' & 'Dietary Fiber.' With these nutrients, the recommended daily values of these quantities, per McDonalds' standards, can be obtained & then compared to the current (2025) daily nutrient recommendations from the US FDA.

In [3]:
#Obtain recommended nutrient amounts for the variables with the necessary data
#make a new dataset
df_recom_nutrients = orig_df.copy()

#get recommended daily TOTAL FAT from McD's data
df_recom_nutrients['REC Total Fat'] = df_recom_nutrients.apply(lambda x: 
            x['Total Fat']*(100/x['Total Fat (% Daily Value)']) if x['Total Fat (% Daily Value)'] != 0 else np.nan, 
                                                               axis=1)
#SATURATED FAT
df_recom_nutrients['REC Saturated Fat'] = df_recom_nutrients.apply(lambda x: 
            x['Saturated Fat']*(100/x['Saturated Fat (% Daily Value)']) if x['Saturated Fat (% Daily Value)'] != 0 else np.nan, 
                                                               axis=1)
#CHOLESTEROL
df_recom_nutrients['REC Cholesterol'] = df_recom_nutrients.apply(lambda x: 
            x['Cholesterol']*(100/x['Cholesterol (% Daily Value)']) if x['Cholesterol (% Daily Value)'] != 0 else np.nan, 
                                                               axis=1)
#SODIUM
df_recom_nutrients['REC Sodium'] = df_recom_nutrients.apply(lambda x: 
            x['Sodium']*(100/x['Sodium (% Daily Value)']) if x['Sodium (% Daily Value)'] != 0 else np.nan, 
                                                               axis=1)
#CARBOHYDRATES
df_recom_nutrients['REC Carbohydrates'] = df_recom_nutrients.apply(lambda x: 
            x['Carbohydrates']*(100/x['Carbohydrates (% Daily Value)']) if x['Carbohydrates (% Daily Value)'] != 0 else np.nan, 
                                                               axis=1)
#DIETARY FIBER
df_recom_nutrients['REC Dietary Fiber'] = df_recom_nutrients.apply(lambda x: 
            x['Dietary Fiber']*(100/x['Dietary Fiber (% Daily Value)']) if x['Dietary Fiber (% Daily Value)'] != 0 else np.nan, 
                                                               axis=1)
#select columns of interest
df_recom_nutrients = df_recom_nutrients[['Category','Item','REC Total Fat','REC Saturated Fat','REC Cholesterol',
                                         'REC Sodium','REC Carbohydrates','REC Dietary Fiber']]

The data tables above indicate recommended amounts of daily nutrients for a typical diet. The first is from the US FDA, whereas the latter pertains to aggregate estimates from the McDonalds menu. Only six quantities were compared because they were the only ones with sufficient data from the provided dataset with which obtain such recommendations.

To compare each nutrient, the median values were used.

  • McDonalds' recommended Total Fat value is noticeably less than that of the US FDA's recommended value; ~ 65 vs 78g.
  • McDonalds' recommended Saturated Fat value is essentially identical to that of the US FDA's recommended value; 20g.
  • McDonalds' recommended Cholesterol value is about equal to that of the US FDA's recommended value; ~ 298 vs 300mg.
  • McDonalds' recommended Sodium value is slightly greater than that of the US FDA's recommended value; ~ 2400 vs 2300mg.
  • McDonalds' recommended Carbohydrates value is noticeably greater than that of the US FDA's recommended value; ~ 300 vs 275g.
  • McDonalds' recommended Dietary Fiber value is slightly less than that of the US FDA's recommended value; ~ 25 vs 28g.

From this information, the differences in the recommended daily values of nutrients per McDonalds' standards & those of the US FDA display generally consistent patterns overall. Moreover, there are no gross differences in magnitude between these different recommended quantities--the largest difference is 25 grams (carbohydrates)--so the McDonalds' recommended daily nutrients can be described as acceptable for the purposes of these analyses. In other words, the daily nutritional values, as quantified by this McDonalds' dataset, do describe a relatively healthy daily diet.

Analysis I - Rich Foods¶

Find foods that exceed any recommended nutritional daily value.

Some columns in the dataset describe a nutritional value relative to a recommended daily value such as 'Total Fat (% Daily Value)'. As an example, if some food item had a 'Total Fat (% Daily Value)' of 60, it implies that a single serving of this item accounts for 60% of the recommended daily amount of total fat for a typical diet. If this daily value exceeded 100 percent, then the recommended daily amount for that nutrient has been exceeded, at least according to McDonalds' recommendations.

The greater this value, the more unhealthy such items tend to be because of how disproportionately they account for specific nutrients. Typically, people consume multiple items throughout a day, many of which contain some amount of various nutrients. For example, if someone consumes 95 percent of their recommended daily total fat from a single item, that item would not be considered to be generally healthy for a typical diet. It will likely be challenging for someone to consume five percent or less in total fat & adequate amounts of other nutrients in addition to such an item for the rest of a day. In other words, if an item is very rich in certain nutrients & not in others, it makes following a balanced diet more challenging throughout a day.

For the purposes of these analyses, items that accounted for the entirety of a typical diet's nutrients or more were identified. Depending on the serving size & quantities of other nutrients of the food item, it would provide a general sense as to how healthy or unhealthy such an item might be. Since these daily-value estimates are based off of a daily diet that consumes 2,000 calories, such a diet was considered to be generally "healthy" for the purposes of this analysis; however, that is not to say that all other diets are unequivocally unhealthy.

Ultimately, daily consumption levels aren't perfect nor is following such a diet to a tee, but the closer that individuals are in approaching or consuming around recommended daily quantities of nutrients, the more healthy they are likely to be. Various individuals have different needs & desires in terms of how they want to consume food & nutrients; however, there are definitely levels of healthy & unhealthy when it comes to a balanced diet. Moreover, the nature of the nutrient is an important factor to consider given that some are relatively healthier than others. For example, high amounts of fat can lead to unhealthy body compositions & health risks, whereas large amounts of protein can help build muscle & strength.
On the US FDA's website, they advise to consume foods that are higher in dietary fiber & lower in saturated fat, sodium, & added sugars. Additionally, when it comes to percentages of daily values, their general guide states that five percent of a recommended daily value or less of a nutrient per serving is considered low, whereas 20% or more is considered high.

In [5]:
#Obtain columns that pertain to a daily value (DV) percentage
DV_cols = [col for col in orig_df.columns if re.search('% Daily Value', col)]

#Find food items that exceed the recommended % DV of any nutrition
    #can use pandas.ge(x) (greater than or equal to x)
data_I = orig_df[orig_df[DV_cols].ge(100).any(axis=1)]
display(data_I.reset_index(drop=True).drop(columns=['Calories from Fat','Total Fat','Saturated Fat', 'Trans Fat',
                                        'Cholesterol','Sodium','Carbohydrates','Dietary Fiber','Sugars','Protein']))

The data_I variable contains food items from the McDonalds menu that exceed any nutrients in a single serving based on recommended daily values, at least according to McDonalds' menu. Such items can be said to generally be unhealthy because of how disproportionately they account for one or more nutrients in a typical daily diet. Given that people usually consume multiple items in a day, consuming one that is rich in one or more nutrients will make consuming a balanced diet in a day more challenging because many foods generally possess multiple different nutrients.

Of the 260 food items in the menu, 21 of them exceed one or more nutrients in terms of how much they account for in a single serving. In this selection of items, the nutrients which saw excessive amounts in a single serving include total fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, vitamin A, & vitamin C. Of these items, seven are breakfast foods, six are salads, & four are beverages.
There are only two food items that exceed a daily recommended amount across multiple nutrients.

  • One serving of "Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Large Biscuit)" accounts for about 100 percent of a typical daily diet's recommended saturated fat level & about 192 percent of the recommended daily amount of cholesterol.
  • One serving of the "40-piece Chicken McNuggets" accounts for about 182 percent of a typical daily diet's recommended total fat level, about 101 percent of the recommended daily amount of saturated fat, & about 150 percent of the recommended daily amount of sodium.

To further illustrate how such foods can lead to an unbalanced &/or unhealthy diet, consider the "Big Breakfast (Regular Biscuit)" food item. One serving of this item accounts for about 740 calories, which is 37% of a 2,000 calorie diet. As such, someone who consumes such an item will likely be eating additional items throughout their day. Nonetheless, this item accounts for about 73% of the recommended daily amount of total fat, 87% of saturated fat, & 185% of cholesterol. Moreover, it only accounts for about 17% of carbohydrates, 12% of dietary fiber, two percent of vitamin C, & 15% of calcium.
In seeking a balanced diet across most nutrients, an individual who eats this item would need to consume foods with low amounts of fat & cholesterol over the rest of their day that also contain more carbohydrates, fiber, & calcium. There are certainly food items in which this could be accomplished, but by consuming the Big Breakfast with the Regular Biscuit, not only does it put the consumer "over their daily limit" for the day when it comes to cholesterol, but it also compromises what other foods they might eat over the rest of the day if they are trying to follow a balanced diet.

With this in mind, if customers are looking to avoid consuming excessive amounts of certain nutrients, they would be advised to avoid these foods or get them in smaller quantities particularly those that are high in saturated fat, sodium, & added sugars.

Analysis II - Rich Foods by Nutrient¶

Find the five food items with the most nutritional value across each nutrient.

When analyzing foods rich in nutrients, another interpretation in how they can contribute to a person's diet is that they can help satisfy "daily quotas" across various nutrients, particularly when it comes to less common nutrients that aren't as common in most foods such as vitamins, iron, or calcium. By identifying such foods from the McDonalds menu, not only can it help educate consumers as to how rich they are across various nutrients, but it can also help point to items that can help people achieve sufficient amounts of certain nutrients or avoid consuming too much.

There are 15 unique nutritional elements in the dataset, but 'Calories from Fat' was not included in this analysis. Bar plots can be made to illustrate the five food items with the most nutritional value across each nutrient. For clarity, these items will be based on a single serving.

The plots above display the five food items across each nutrient that are the most abundant (excluding 'Calories from Fat') for that particular nutritional element. There are 260 unique food items in the dataset. Note that the first ten plots represent absolute nutritional quantities whereas the bottom four plots display percentages with respect to McDonalds' daily nutritional recommendations. Further, the vertical axes of each plot are unique & are unrelated to those of other plots.
Some notes concerning the items across each plot are listed below.

Calories¶

  • The 40-piece Chicken McNuggets contains the most calories of any item on the McDonalds menu; 1,880. If a typical diet is recommended to consist of around 2,000 calories a day, then this food item would account for nearly all of this allotment. For those wanting to pursue a balanced diet, this item would not be a good recommendation in terms of consuming a balanced amount of calories.
  • The next richest food from McDonalds in terms of calories is the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes with a Large Biscuit (1,150 calories). Apart from the 40-piece Chicken McNuggets, McDonalds items generally aren't too overwhelming in terms of their calorie abundance, but many can still be heavy.

Total Fat¶

  • The 40-piece Chicken McNuggets contains the most fat of any item on the McDonalds menu; 118 grams (g). Based on the US FDA's nutritional recommendations in 2025, the daily recommendation of total fat is 78 g. The 40-piece Chicken McNuggets is the only food item on the menu that exceeds or meets this daily recommendation. As such, this item would not be a good recommendation in terms of consuming a balanced amount of fat.
  • The next richest food from McDonalds in terms of total fat is the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes with a Large Biscuit (60 g). Apart from the 40-piece Chicken McNuggets, McDonalds items generally aren't too overwhelming in terms of their abundance of total fat, but many can still be quite heavy.

Saturated Fat¶

  • There are four items on the McDonalds menu with the largest amount of saturated fat: the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Large Biscuit), 40-piece Chicken McNuggets, Large Frappé Chocolate Chip, & Medium McFlurry with M&M's Candies each have 20 g of saturated fat. The daily recommendation of saturated fat is 20 g, so each of these food items would meet this threshold in a single serving. As such, these items would not be a good recommendation in terms of consuming a balanced amount of saturated fat.
  • There are many McDonalds items which are very heavy in their abundance of saturated fat. This is particularly concerning given that the US FDA warns specifically against consuming foods that are higher in saturated fat.

Trans Fat¶

  • A Double Quarter Pounder with Cheese contains the most trans fat of any item on the McDonalds menu; 2.5 g. The daily recommendation of trans fat is to limit it to less than one percent of total energy intake. Given that this analysis is based off of a 2,000 calorie diet, this threshold would fall at about 2.2 g, indicating that a single serving of this food item would exceed this daily recommendation by a small margin. This is the only food item on the menu that exceeds or meets this daily recommendation. As such, this item would not be a good recommendation in terms of consuming a balanced amount of trans fat; however, given that trans fat is less common amongst most foods across the nutrients involved here, 2.5 g of it wouldn't be terribly consequential as long as other items that are eaten during a day don't possess much, if any, trans fat.
  • The next richest food from McDonalds in terms of trans fat is Steak, Egg & Cheese Bagel (1.5 g). Apart from the Double Quarter Pounder with Cheese, McDonalds items generally aren't too overwhelming in terms of their abundance of trans fat, but many can still be fairly heavy.

Cholesterol¶

  • There are two items on the McDonalds menu with the largest amount of cholesterol: the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Regular Biscuit) & the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Large Biscuit) each have 575 milligrams (mg) of cholesterol. The daily recommendation of cholesterol is 300 mg, so both of these food items would exceed this daily threshold significantly. Additionally, there are three other items on the menu that meet or exceed this daily recommendation: Big Breakfast (Regular Biscuit) & Big Breakfast (Large Biscuit) (555 mg), Steak & Egg McMuffin (300 mg). As such, the Big Breakfast items in particular would not be good recommendations in terms of consuming a balanced amount of cholesterol.
  • There are many McDonalds items which are very heavy in their abundance of cholesterol.

Sodium¶

  • The 40-piece Chicken McNuggets contains the most sodium of any item on the McDonalds menu; 3,600 milligrams (mg). The daily recommendation of sodium is 2,300 mg, so this food item would exceed this threshold significantly. This is the only food item on the menu that exceeds or meets this daily recommendation. As such, this item would not be a good recommendation in terms of consuming a balanced amount of sodium.
  • The next richest food from McDonalds in terms of sodium is the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes and Egg Whites with a Large Biscuit (2,290 mg). Even after excluding the 40-piece Chicken McNuggets, there are many McDonalds items that are very heavy in terms of their abundance of sodium. This is particularly concerning given that the US FDA warns specifically against consuming foods that are higher in sodium.

Carbohydrates¶

  • A Large Chocolate Shake contains the most carbohydrates of any item on the McDonalds menu; 141 g. The daily recommendation of carbohydrates is 275 g, so this food item only contains about half of this quantity. As such, this item would not necessarily be a bad recommendation in terms of consuming a balanced amount of carbohydrates, but it still fairly heavy.
  • The next richest food from McDonalds in terms of carbohydrates is the Large Strawberry Shake (140 g). In fact, large smoothies & shakes are generally the richest foods from McDonalds in terms of carbohydrates, but these abundances are quite similar (around 130 g). Although McDonalds items aren't overwhelming in terms of their abundance of carbohydrates, many are still fairly heavy, particularly large smoothies & shakes.

Dietary Fiber¶

  • There are four items on the McDonalds menu with the largest amount of dietary fiber of all items: the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Large Biscuit), Big Breakfast with Hotcakes & Egg Whites (Large Biscuit), Premium Southwest Salad with Crispy Chicken, & Premium Southwest Salad with Gilled Chicken each have seven grams of dietary fiber. The daily recommendation of dietary fiber is 28 g, so these foods only equate to a quarter of this daily quantity each. As such, these items wouldn't be bad recommendations in terms of consuming a balanced amount of dietary fiber.
  • Most McDonalds items seem to underwhelm when it comes to containing considerable amounts of dietary fiber suggesting that McDonalds items aren't a good or reliable source of this nutrient. This is particularly concerning given that the US FDA encourages consumers to choose foods specifically higher in dietary fiber.

Sugars¶

  • A Medium McFlurry with M&M's Candies contains the most added sugars of any item on the McDonalds menu; 128 g. The daily recommendation of sugars is 50 g, so this food item would exceed this threshold by about 250%. As such, this item would not be a good recommendation in terms of consuming a balanced amount of sugars.
  • There are 63 items on the McDonalds menu that meet or exceed this daily recommendation of 50 g of added sugars, most of which are either in the Coffee & Tea or Smoothies & Shakes category. As such, it can be said that many McDonalds items are overwhelming in terms of their abundance of sugars. This is particularly concerning given that the US FDA warns specifically against consuming foods that are higher in sugars.

Protein¶

  • The 40-piece Chicken McNuggets contains the most protein of any item on the McDonalds menu; 87 g. The daily recommendation of protein is 50 g, so this food item exceeds this quantity significantly. This is the only item that meets or exceeds this daily recommendation of protein. As such, this item would not be a good recommendation in terms of consuming a balanced amount of protein.
  • The next richest food from McDonalds in terms of protein is the Double Quarter Pounder with Cheese (48 g). Apart from the 40-piece Chicken McNuggets, several McDonalds items seem to offer heavy amounts of protein. For people following a more balanced diet, such items would not be ideal recommendations, but for those who want more protein in their diet, McDonalds certainly has several strong items to choose from.

Vitamin A (% Daily Value)¶

  • There are three items on the McDonalds menu with the largest amount of Vitamin A as a percentage of daily value for a typical diet: the Premium Bacon Ranch Salad (without Chicken), Premium Southwest Salad with Crispy Chicken, & Premium Southwest Salad with Grilled Chicken each contain 170% of the recommended daily value of Vitamin A. In total, there are six items on the menu that exceed the recommended daily value of Vitamin A, all of which are salads. For reference, the daily recommendation of Vitamin A, per the US FDA, is 900 micrograms (mcg).
  • Given this, it can be said that several McDonalds items, particularly salads, are very heavy in terms of their abundance of vitamin A.

Vitamin C (% Daily Value)¶

  • The Large Minute Maid Orange Juice contains the largest amount of Vitamin C as a percentage of daily value for a typical diet; 240%. In total, there are seven items on the menu that exceed the recommended daily value of Vitamin C, all of which include some fruit. Many of these items are beverages. For reference, the daily recommendation of Vitamin C is 90 mg.
  • The next richest food from McDonalds in terms of Vitamin C is the Apple Slices (160% of the recommended daily value). Even after excluding the Large Minute Maid Orange Juice, there are many McDonalds items that are very heavy in terms of their abundance of Vitamin C.

Calcium (% Daily Value)¶

  • There are two items on the McDonalds menu with the largest amount of Calcium as a percentage of daily value for a typical diet: the Large Strawberry Shake & Medium McFlurry with M&M's Candies both contain 70% of the recommended daily value of Calcium. For reference, the daily recommendation of Calcium is 1,300 mg.
  • The next richest items from McDonalds in terms of Calcium include other coffees, teas, smoothies, & shakes (60% of the recommended daily value). As such, while there are no items that are overwhelming in terms of their abundance of calcium, many are fairly heavy. This is encouraging given that the US FDA encourages consumers to choose foods specifically higher in calcium.

Iron (% Daily Value)¶

  • There are two items on the McDonalds menu with the largest amount of Iron as a percentage of daily value for a typical diet: the Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Regular Biscuit) & Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Large Biscuit) both contain 40% of the recommended daily value of Iron. For reference, the daily recommendation of Iron is 18 mg.
  • The next richest food from McDonalds in terms of Iron is the Double Quarter Pounder with Cheese (35% of the recommended daily value). As such, there aren't any foods that are heavy in iron, but there are several that include a considerable amount that can help contribute to a balanced diet. This is slightly concerning given that the US FDA encourages consumers to choose foods specifically higher in iron.

The 40-piece Chicken McNuggets has the most nutritional value for four different nutrients (calories, total fat, sodium, protein) which is more than any other food item on the McDonalds menu. Other items with significantly large values across multiple nutrients include: Big Breakfast with Hotcakes (Large & Regular Biscuits), Medium McFlurry w/M&M's Candies, Premium Southwest Salad with Crispy Chicken, Premium Southwest Salad with Gilled Chicken, Large Strawberry Shake, Large Chocolate Shake, & other Big Breakfast food items.

Based on these assessments, McDonalds seems to offer several items that are generally either very rich, moderately heavy, or underwhelming in terms of their nutritional abundances across the nutrients analyzed.

  • Nutrients in which several McDonalds items are generally very rich in include: Saturated Fat, Cholesterol, Sodium, Sugars, Vitamin A, & Vitamin C. This is particularly problematic given that the US FDA advises specifically against consuming higher levels of saturated fat, sodium, & added sugars.
  • Nutrients in which several McDonalds items are generally moderately heavy in include: Calories, Total Fat, Trans Fat, Carbohydrates, Protein, & Calcium. Given that the US FDA advises people to choose foods that are higher in calcium, this pattern is encouraging.
  • Nutrients in which several McDonalds items are generally underwhelming include: Dietary Fiber & Iron. This is also problematic given that the US FDA advises people to consume higher levels of dietary fiber & iron.

With this in mind, people who are desiring to follow a balanced diet would be advised that they may need to be more strict in what they consume from McDonalds when it comes to saturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, sugars, vitamin A, & vitamin C. They would also be advised that there are several items that are moderately heavy in calories, total fat, trans fat, carbohydrates, protein, & calcium. On the other hand, such customers don't necessarily have to be concerned about consuming excessive levels of dietary fiber & iron when eating from McDonalds; however, customers who want to consume more fiber &/or iron than a typical diet may recommend may find McDonalds' selection of items insufficient.
When evaluated against specific recommendations from the US FDA, these analyses seem to indicate that McDonalds foods provide unhealthy amounts of saturated fat, sodium, & sugars & insufficient amounts of dietary fiber & iron. Furthermore, McDonalds foods only seem satisfactory when it comes to calcium levels.

Analysis III - Nutrients by Food Category¶

Inspect the typical amount of each nutrient per category of the McDonalds menu.

Breaking down nutritional abundances by category in the McDonalds menu can help reveal typical nutritional compositions of such items. Depending on these distributions, it can potentially be helpful in how customers can consume a more balanced collection of foods when eating at McDonalds. For example, if a customer consumes an item high in cholesterol, having an understanding of nutrients in other foods can help assist them in assessing what other items they could eat that aren't as high in cholesterol. Such information could also be useful for people who are following more particular diets such as high-protein or low-fat diets.

There are nine unique categories in the dataset each of which accounts for between six (Salads) & 95 (Coffee & Tea) food items on the menu. When assessing measures of centrality, the median can be used given that it is less sensitive to outliers.

#Define columns of interest
data_III_cols = ['Calories','Calories from Fat','Total Fat','Saturated Fat','Trans Fat','Cholesterol','Sodium',
                 'Carbohydrates','Dietary Fiber','Sugars','Protein','Vitamin A (% Daily Value)','Vitamin C (% Daily Value)',
                'Calcium (% Daily Value)','Iron (% Daily Value)']
#calculate avg nutrition per 'Category', round to 2 decimals
cat_means = orig_df.groupby('Category')[data_III_cols].mean().reset_index().round(2)
#indicate the statistic
cat_means['Metric'] = 'Average'

#calculate median nutrition per 'Category', round to 2 decimals
cat_meds = orig_df.groupby('Category')[data_III_cols].median().reset_index().round(2)
#indicate the statistic
cat_meds['Metric'] = 'Median'

#determine # unique food items each category accounts for
cat_counts = orig_df.Category.value_counts().reset_index()

#merge category means, medians, & counts together, sort
data_III = pd.concat([cat_means, cat_meds], axis=0).merge(cat_counts, on='Category').sort_values('Category').rename(
                columns={'count':'# items'}).reset_index(drop=True)

#reorganize columns
data_III = data_III[['Category','# items','Metric','Calories','Calories from Fat','Total Fat','Saturated Fat','Trans Fat',
                    'Cholesterol','Sodium','Carbohydrates','Dietary Fiber','Sugars','Protein','Vitamin A (% Daily Value)',
                     'Vitamin C (% Daily Value)','Calcium (% Daily Value)','Iron (% Daily Value)']]
data_III.head(4)

The plots above display typical quantities of nutritional elements in foods according to the category on the McDonalds menu. In this case, these plots specifically illustrate the median values per category for all 15 of the nutrients in the dataset except 'Calories from Fat.' Recall that there are nine unique categories of food items in the dataset, each of which consist of somewhere between six & 95 unique items. Note that the vertical axis of each plots is different to that of the others.

Recall that the US FDA encourages people to consume foods that are higher in dietary fiber & lower in saturated fat, sodium, & added sugars. Additionally, when it comes to percentages of daily values, their general guide states that five percent of a recommended daily value or less of a nutrient per serving is considered low, whereas 20% or more is considered high.

Calories¶

  • Typically, foods in the Smoothies & Shakes category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most calories of any of the nine categories; about 540 calories. Recall that a daily diet is recommended to consist of 2,000 calories. As such, a typical smoothy or shake from McDonalds would account for about a quarter of a person's daily calorie count which is considerable but not overwhelmingly unhealthy.
  • Beef & Pork, Breakfast, & Chicken & Fish items from McDonalds also typically have a relatively high number of calories. Conversely, McDonalds Beverages have the lowest number of calories of any of the nine categories; about 100 calories which is less than half of that of any other food category.

Total Fat¶

  • Typically, foods in the Beef & Pork & Breakfast categories of items on the McDonalds menu have the most fat of the nine categories; about 26 grams (g) each. Recall that a daily diet is recommended to consist of 78 g of total fat. As such, a typical food item from either of these two categories would account for about a third of a person's daily total fat intake which is fairly considerable but not overwhelmingly unhealthy.
  • Chicken & Fish items from McDonalds also typically have a relatively high amount of fat. Conversely, McDonalds Beverages have the lowest amount of total fat of any of the nine categories; about zero g.

Saturated Fat¶

  • Typically, foods in the Breakfast category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most saturated fat of any of the nine categories; about 11 g. Recall that a daily diet is recommended to consist of 20 g of saturated fat. As such, a typical breakfast food from McDonalds would account for about half of a person's daily saturated fat intake which is considerable. Given that the US FDA advises customers to avoid items particurlarly higher in saturated fat, Breakfast items would not be ideal for people pursuing a balanced/healthier diet.
  • Beef & Pork items & Smoothies & Shakes also typically have a relatively high amount of saturated fat. Such items would also be problematic for more balanced diets. Conversely, McDonalds Beverages have the lowest amount of saturated fat of any of the nine categories; about zero g. As such, consumers may be less likely to face health risks if they were to consume these kind of drinks (Beverages) as opposed to smoothies & shakes.

Trans Fat¶

  • Typically, only two categories of the nine in the dataset have items with any trans fat--Beef & Pork & Smoothies & Shakes--each of which typically have one gram or less of trans fat. Recall that a daily diet is recommended to limit trans fat to less than one percent of total energy intake. For a 2,000 calorie diet, this would equate to about 2.2 g. As such, most categories are relatively healthy in this regard; however, choosing multiple items from these two categories would generally be discouraged.

Cholesterol¶

  • Typically, foods in the Beef & Pork category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most cholesterol of any of the nine categories; about 85 milligrams (mg). Recall that a daily diet is recommended to consist of 300 mg of cholesterol. As such, a typical food item from this category would account for about 30% of a person's daily cholesterol intake which is notable but not super unhealthy.
  • Chicken & Fish & Salads items from McDonalds also typically have relatively notable amounts of cholesterol. Conversely, McDonalds Beverages have the lowest amount of cholesterol of any of the nine categories; about zero mg.

Sodium¶

  • Typically, foods in the Breakfast category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most sodium of any of the nine categories; about 1,265 mg. Recall that a daily diet is recommended to consist of 2,300 mg of sodium. As such, a typical breakfast food from McDonalds would account for about half of a person's daily sodium intake which is considerable. Given that the US FDA advises customers to avoid items particurlarly higher in sodium, Breakfast items would not be ideal for people pursuing a balanced/healthier diet.
  • Chicken & Fish & Beef & Pork items from McDonalds also typically have a relatively high amount of sodium. Such items would also be problematic for more balanced diets. Conversely, McDonalds Beverages have the lowest amount of sodium of any of the nine categories; about 30 mg.

Carbohydrates¶

  • Typically, foods in the Smoothies & Shakes category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most carbohydrates of any of the nine categories; about 88 g. Recall that a daily diet is recommended to consist of 275 g of carbs. As such, a typical smoothy/shake from McDonalds would account for nearly a third of a person's daily carb intake which is notable but not very unhealthy.
  • The next highest category in terms of typical amounts of carbohydrates is Breakfast & Coffee & Tea items at about 45 g which is certainly more acceptable. Conversely, McDonalds Salads have the lowest amount of carbs of any of the nine categories; about 21 g.

Dietary Fiber¶

  • Typically, foods in the Salads category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most dietary fiber of any of the nine categories; about 4.5 grams. Recall that a daily diet is recommended to consist of 28 g of dietary fiber. As such, a typical breakfast food from McDonalds would account for less than a fifth of a person's daily dietary fiber intake which is quite underwhelming. Given that the US FDA advises customers to consume items particurlarly higher in dietary fiber, Salads items typically provide the best options for customers pursuing a balanced/healthier diet in this regard.
  • Beef & Pork, Breakfast, & Chicken & Fish items from McDonalds also typically have decent amounts of dietary fiber among the categories (three grams each); however, they are still somewhat insufficient when it comes to what is recommended daily. Conversely, McDonalds Beverages have the least dietary fiber of any of the nine categories; about zero g.

Added Sugars¶

  • Typically, foods in the Smoothies & Shakes category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most added sugars of any of the nine categories; about 75 grams. Recall that a daily diet is recommended to consist of 50 g of sugars. As such, a typical breakfast food from McDonalds would account for about 150% of a person's daily sugar intake which is overwhelmingly unhealthy. Given that the US FDA advises customers to avoid items particurlarly higher in added sugars, Smoothies & Shakes would not be ideal for people pursuing a balanced/healthier diet.
  • Coffee & Tea items from McDonalds also typically have higher amounts of sugars (about 40 g). Conversely, McDonalds Snacks & Sides have the lowest amount of sugars of any of the nine categories; about two g. This is more or less a harmful amount of sugars & more ideal for a healthier diet.

Protein¶

  • Typically, foods in the Chicken & Fish category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most protein of any of the nine categories; about 27 g. Recall that a daily diet is recommended to consist of 50 g of protein. As such, a typical item from this category would account for half of a person's daily protein intake which is notable but not overwhelming.
  • Beef & Pork & Salads items from McDonalds also typically have more amounts of protein (nearly 25 g). Conversely, McDonalds Beverages have the least protein of any of the nine categories; about zero g.

Vitamin A (% Daily Value)¶

  • Typically, foods in the Salads category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most Vitamin A of any of the nine categories; about 165% of the daily value of a typical diet which is excessive.
  • No other category typically contains more than 25% of the daily value of a typical diet. Furthermore, McDonalds Beverages have the lowest amount of vitamin A of any of the nine categories; about zero micrograms. As such, customers do not have many reliable sources at McDonalds when trying to consume balanced amounts of Vitamin A.

Vitamin C (% Daily Value)¶

  • Typically, foods in the Salads category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most Vitamin C of any of the nine categories; about 30% of the daily value of a typical diet.
  • No other category typically contains 20% of the daily value of a typical diet & only two others typically contain more than five percent. As such, outside of Salads, customers do not have a plethora of reliable sources at McDonalds when trying to consume balanced amounts of Vitamin C.

Calcium (% Daily Value)¶

  • Typically, foods in the Smoothies & Shakes category of items on the McDonalds menu have the most calcium of any of the nine categories; about 40% of the daily value of a typical diet. Given that the US FDA advises customers to consume items particurlarly higher in calcium, Smoothies & Shakes provide the best options for people pursuing a balanced amount of calcium; however, as illustrated from other nutrients, these items aren't generally healthy in other ways.
  • Beef & Pork & Coffee & Tea items from McDonalds also typically have more amounts of calcium (about 25% of the daily value of a typical diet) so they can provide nice options for people trying to consume more calcium. Conversely, McDonalds Beverages have the lowest amount of calcium of any of the nine categories; about zero mg.

Iron (% Daily Value)¶

  • Typically, foods in the Beef & Pork & Chicken & Fish categories of items on the McDonalds menu have the most iron of the nine categories; about 20% of the daily value of a typical diet each. Given that the US FDA recommends customers to consume items higher in iron, Beef & Pork & Chicken & Fish items provide the best options for people pursuing a balanced amount of iron; however, the relatively limited amount in such items may require customers to seek additional foods that are similarly or more rich in iron.
  • Conversely, McDonalds Beverages have the lowest amount of iron of any of the nine categories; about zero mg. Generally, there aren't many reliable sources from McDonalds for customers that desire to consume higher amounts of iron.

Of these 14 nutrients, some categories consistently have some of the largest nutritional abundances.

  • McDonalds Smoothies & Shakes & Beef & Pork items each have the highest typical quantities across four of the 14 nutrients. Smoothies & Shakes are typically the most abundant in calories, carbs, sugars, & calcium, whereas Beef & Pork food items are typically the most abundant in fat, trans fat, cholesterol, & iron.
  • Moreover, Chicken & Fish as well as Breakfast items are also among the richest in terms of nutritional abundance.
  • Conversely, McDonalds Beverages are usually among the least fulfilling of the nine categories across most of these nutrients (11 of 14). Snacks & Sides & Desserts items are also typically less sufficient in supplying high amounts of nutrients across these food categories.

When evaluating categories whose food items typically exceeded daily nutrient recommendations based off of single servings, only sugars & vitamin A were ever exceeded. More specifically, Salads typically exceeded the recommended amount of vitamin A that should be consumed in a day, & Smoothies & Shakes typically exceeded the recommended amount of sugars.
With that being said, there were still some nutrients in which food categories typically contained heavy amounts that didn't necessarily exceed the daily recommendations of the US FDA yet could still be considered relatively unhealthy.

  • A typical Beef & Pork, Breakfast, or Smoothies & Shakes item contained about half the saturated fat (10-11 g) recommended for one day (20 g).
  • A typical Beef & Pork item contained about half the trans fat (1.0 g) recommended for one day (2.2 g).
  • A typical Breakfast & Chicken & Fish item contained more than half the sodium (~ 1,250 mg) recommended for one day (2,300 mg).
  • A typical Beef & Pork, Chicken & Fish, & Salads item contained about half the protein (24-27 g) recommended for one day (50 g).

On the other hand, there were a couple of nutrients in which most categories typically didn't come close to providing sufficient amounts.

  • The category with the highest typical abundance of dietary fiber was Salads at about 4.5 grams. The FDA recommends around 28 grams per day, so many McDonalds foods generally seem to lack adequate amounts of dietary fiber.
  • Other than salads, no other food category typically contained 25% or more of the daily recommended value of vitamin A.
  • The category with the highest typical abundance of vitamin C was Salads at about 30%. No other category typically contained even 20%. As such, many McDonalds foods generally seem to lack adequate amounts of vitamin C.
  • No category typically contained more than 20% of the daily recommended value of iron. As such, many McDonalds foods generally seem to lack adequate amounts of iron.

In regard to the nutrients most emphasized by the US FDA:

  • Breakfast, Beef & Pork, & Smoothies & Shakes items from McDonalds are particularly rich in saturated fat. Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with less saturated fat, such items would generally be considered unhealthy.
  • Breakfast, Chicken & Fish, & Beef & Pork items from McDonalds are fairly rich in sodium. Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with less sodium, such items would generally be considered unhealthy.
  • Smoothies & Shakes & Coffee & Tea items from McDonalds are fairly rich in sugars. Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with less added sugars, such items would generally be considered unhealthy.
  • The greatest abundance in dietary fiber of the nine McDonalds food categories is about 4.5 grams (Salads). Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with more dietary fiber, McDonalds foods generally seem to lack adequate amounts of dietary fiber.
  • Three McDonalds food categories typically contain between 20 to 40 percent of the daily recommended value of calcium; Smoothies & Shakes, Coffee & Tea, & Beef & Pork. While these categories are somewhat sufficient in providing customers with adequate amounts of calcium--a nutrient in which the FDA encourages people to consume more of--the other six categories are not.
  • The greatest abundance in iron of the nine McDonalds food categories is about 20% of the daily recommended value; Beef & Pork, Chicken & Fish. Given that the FDA recommends people to consume foods with more iron, McDonalds foods generally seem to lack adequate amounts of iron.

Analysis IV - Assessing Nutrition of Daily Meals¶

Construct a daily meal plan that doesn't exceed the recommended daily nutritional values; i.e. breakfast, lunch, & dinner. Include at least eight unique food items. Assume that the daily nutritional values are for a 2,000 calorie (daily) diet.

By constructing daily meal plans using various McDonalds foods, it can give an idea as to how healthy McDonalds foods generally are compared to non-fast-food meals & daily diets. Moreover, it can indicate whether McDonalds foods are generally more biased towards certain nutrients or not & whether they are generally capable of providing customers with well-balanced meals.

Given that not all of the daily nutritional recommendations are determinable with the available data, the US FDA's daily recommendations can be used as standards here, the data of which can be obtained via the FDA_daily_nutrients variable. More specifically, the known recommendations are as follows. For the variables that only describe the percentage of a daily value, such as vitamin A, vitamin C, calcium, & iron, their daily recommendations will just be at 100%.
Once more, it's important to point out, as observed prior to Analysis I, that some of the daily recommendations of nutrients differ between McDonalds' menu & the US FDA. As such, specific amounts of certain nutrients, particularly those that are described with a daily value percentage, cannot be determined.

  • Calories: 2,000
  • Calories from Fat: 600
  • Total Fat: 78 g
  • Saturated Fat: 20 g
  • Trans Fat: ~ 2.2g (for a 2,000 calorie diet)
  • Cholesterol: 300 mg
  • Sodium: 2,300 mg
  • Carbohydrates: 275 g
  • Dietary Fiber: 28 g
  • Sugars: 50 g
  • Protein: 50 g

Two approaches were used in this section as listed below. 1) Random daily meals were assembled to evaluate how & if a day's worth of McDonalds food satisfies daily nutritional recommendations. 2) The food items were explored to manually construct a day's worth of McDonalds food such that none of the daily nutritional recommendations were excessively exceeded.

Analysis IV A - Random Daily Meal Plans¶

Before constructing daily meal plans by hand, meals could be amassed by sampling random food items from the dataset. For example, a breakfast & coffee item could be randomly sampled for a typical breakfast meal, a salad & beverage items could be sampled for a lunch, & a chicken, beverage, & dessert item could be sampled for dinner. With these random items, the total nutrients could be calculated & determined whether they exceed the recommended daily values or not.
Assembling multiple meal plans could normalize the results to gain an idea as to how daily meal plans from McDonalds typically contribute towards a consumer's daily nutrition & whether they are generally balanced or not.

To conduct & streamline these processes, a couple of functions can be built. When sampling these random items, a random seed needs to be set to ensure reproducibility. In this case, the 40 piece Chicken McNuggets item was excluded from this analysis because it exceeds the daily recommendation of multiple nutrients. Additionally, this item is the least reasonable item on the menu for a single person to eat in one meal; 40 nuggets is typically not equivalent to a single serving for an average diet.

In this section, ten random daily meal plans were created & analyzed, each of which contains eight food items from the McDonalds menu. Each meal contained a certain number of food items from specific categories in the dataset, which are listed below:

  • For the morning meal (breakfast): One "Coffee & Tea" & one "Breakfast" item.
  • For the midday meal (lunch): One "Beverages", one "Snacks & Sides", & one of "Salads"/"Chicken & Fish"/"Beef & Pork" item.
  • For the end-of-day meal (dinner): One "Beverages", one of "Salads"/"Chicken & Fish"/"Beef & Pork", & one of "Desserts"/"Smoothies & Shakes" item.
In [10]:
#Remove the 40 piece Chicken McNuggets item from this analysis
df_no_40_nugs = orig_df[orig_df.Item != 'Chicken McNuggets (40 piece)']

#Create a function to obtain a day's worth of meals (8 food items) from categories of interest.
    #Don't forget to set random seeds when sampling
def get_random_meal(seed):
    """
    This function samples eight random items from the McDonalds menu. Two of these items are in either of the 
    "Salads"/"Chicken & Fish"/"Beef & Pork" categories on the menu, two are in either of the "Desserts"/"Smoothies & Shakes"
    categories, two are in the "Beverages" category, & one is in each of the "Coffee & Tea", "Breakfast", "Snacks & Sides" 
    categories. The data for all of these items is then compiled into a single pandas DataFrame.
    The function takes one input: a random seed which must be an integer.
    """
    #Return a TypeError if the inputted argument is not an integer
    if not isinstance(seed, int):
        raise TypeError("Input must be an integer.")
    
    #Compile data for 8 random food items. For each meal, sample items without replacement so people can have the same thing 
        # twice if desired.
    random_meal = pd.concat([df_no_40_nugs[df_no_40_nugs.Category == 'Coffee & Tea'].sample(1, random_state=seed, replace=False),
                        df_no_40_nugs[df_no_40_nugs.Category == 'Breakfast'].sample(1, random_state=seed, replace=False),
                        df_no_40_nugs[df_no_40_nugs.Category == 'Snacks & Sides'].sample(1, random_state=seed, replace=False),
                        df_no_40_nugs[df_no_40_nugs.Category == 'Beverages'].sample(2, random_state=seed, replace=False),
                        df_no_40_nugs[df_no_40_nugs.Category.str.contains('Salads|Chicken & Fish|Beef & Pork')].sample(2,
                                                        random_state=seed, replace=False),
                        df_no_40_nugs[df_no_40_nugs.Category.str.contains('Desserts|Smoothies & Shakes')].sample(1,
                                                        random_state=seed, replace=False)], axis=0).reset_index(drop=True)
    #return the data for the sampled food items
    return random_meal
In [11]:
#Want to make another function to analyze the data of daily meals

#Filter the `FDA_daily_nutrients` data to relevant nutrients
FDA_IV = FDA_daily_nutrients[~FDA_daily_nutrients.Nutrient.isin(['Biotin','Chloride','Choline','Chromium','Copper',
                                'Folate/Folic Acid','Iodine','Magnesium','Manganese','Molybdenum','Niacin',
                                'Pantothenic Acid','Phosphorus','Potassium','Riboflavin','Selenium','Thiamin','Vitamin B12',
                                'Vitamin B6','Vitamin D','Vitamin E','Vitamin K','Zinc'])].reset_index(drop=True)
#Make the function
def analyze_random_meal(meal_df):
    """
    This function takes some McDonalds food data of one or more meals & evaluates whether the total nutrients exceeds the 
    daily recommended values by the US FDA. The resulting analyses are returned in a single pandas DataFrame.
    This function takes one input: a pandas DataFrame.
    """
    #return a TypeError if the inputted argument is not a pandas DataFrame
    if not isinstance(meal_df, pd.DataFrame):
        raise TypeError("Input must be a pandas DataFrame.")
    
    #Calculate sums of nutrients across all meals
    meal_totals = meal_df.select_dtypes(include='number').sum().reset_index().rename(columns={'index':'Nutrient', 
                                                                                    0:'Meal Total'})
    
    #Merge FDA's daily recommendations & the inputted meals' nutrient totals. Need to manually merge 'Vitamin A', 'Vitamin C',
        # 'Calcium', 'Iron' data points because their names are inconsistent in the 2 datasets.
        #Fill the missing values with 100 (%)--these arise because the daily recommendations for the 4 nutrients above are 
            # unknown since McDonalds only describes them relative to percentages of daily values.
    meal_and_FDA = pd.concat([FDA_IV.merge(meal_totals, on='Nutrient'),
                             meal_totals[meal_totals.Nutrient.str.contains('Vitamin A|Vitamin C|Calcium|Iron')]], 
                            axis=0).fillna('100').sort_values('Nutrient').reset_index(drop=True)
    
    #In the 'Current Daily Value' column, remove non-numerical characters, & convert the column to a numerical type.
    meal_and_FDA['Current Daily Value'] = meal_and_FDA['Current Daily Value'].str.replace(r'[a-z]', '', 
                                                                regex=True).astype('float')
    
    #Create a new column indicating whether the recommended daily value has been exceeded.
    meal_and_FDA['Daily Value Exceeded?'] = meal_and_FDA['Current Daily Value'] < meal_and_FDA['Meal Total']
    
    #Return the daily meal data & its analyses
    return meal_and_FDA

meal_X_results = analyze_random_meal(meal_X)

#Assign a daily-meal-plan identifier to each dataset to distinguish them
for df, i in zip([meal_I_results, meal_II_results, meal_III_results, meal_IV_results, meal_V_results, meal_VI_results,
                  meal_VII_results, meal_VIII_results, meal_IX_results, meal_X_results], range(1,11,1)):
    df['Daily Meal ID'] = i

#Combine all daily meal data; 150 rows = 15 nutrients * 10 meals
all_meal_results = pd.concat([i for i in [meal_I_results, meal_II_results, meal_III_results, meal_IV_results, meal_V_results, 
                            meal_VI_results, meal_VII_results, meal_VIII_results, meal_IX_results, meal_X_results]], 
                                     axis=0).reset_index(drop=True)
display(all_meal_results.sample(3))
